utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if a target walks on a -- in a public place from crossing the street, why not wait until she's in the middle of the street, if that is comfortable as in view of the position of my weapon at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in this instance, I believe that the girls were talking to -- they were warned by the soldiers so they were probably standing at the corner and standing -- a static target is always better than a walking target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is rather speculative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's speculative, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it is not that the shooter would have known the conversation which took place at a quite a distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But he would have seen that the target would have been static for -- for a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- yes. But it's -- you would agree with me that your logic is involving a lot of speculative elements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's speculative but based on experience, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That -- Please move on, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are, I think, at the time for the break, but -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we are approximately at the time of the break because we started approximately one hour ago. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six minutes. Then I am also looking at Mr. Mladic, whether it would be preferable to, first, continue for six minutes and then take the break. The Chamber is willing to take the break now, whatever is preferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're able to continue, according to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, I said we started an hour ago. We started 54 minutes ago. We started after 11.00. We were late. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can call up 1D527 briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, does this intersection look familiar to you? Is it, in fact, the intersection near the vicinity of the place of the incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My visit was in 2009. I don't -- I couldn't say for sure. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In respect to the incident site, did you agree that -- would you agree that there were potential directions of fire, in addition from the direction of the house of the blind, that there was a clear trajectory from Dobrinja or the opposite direction from Dobrinja as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree there were no potential directions of fire, but I could not say the -- as for Dobrinja, if that was -- I couldn't say that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the pockmarks on the building in this photograph, first of all, in your opinion, could that be evidence of a -- that this location was the recipient of a significant exchange of fire between the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing a lot of buildings in Sarajevo that looked like this and had a lot of bullet-holes in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want you to focus on the buildings that you saw in the area of the incident site for this particular incident. Were there a lot of buildings that were pockmarked in this manner in that area when you visited?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and now I ask you: In your opinion, could those pockmarks be evidence that this location was a recipient of significant exchange of fire between the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, over the time that the conflict took place, over that time, those shots would have been collected, but I don't know if that was done in -- within a week, which would have been very intense, or over the course of months or years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess I should tender this photograph based upon the questions about the building; but I do not, at this time, intend to rely upon the markings of the locations. That will have to wait for another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we'd have to know exactly where the picture is taken and what it depicts. Is there any dispute about the pockmarks on the building, that are the traces of fire?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: No, Judge. I wouldn't dispute the pockmarks as to the location. Obviously I would have an objection for it coming in -- as to the precise locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, do you want to tender it now or not? Or would you wait for a later moment? If you want to tender it, we need more details about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could I at least get it MFI'd so that we don't lose the discussion that this witness has had with respect to it or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be fair. Mr. Registrar, the MFI number this document would receive, this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D126, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification as 126. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I earlier asked you, sir, if you knew how far the confrontation line was from this location. I believe you said you did not. Did you at least know the direction the confrontation line was from the incident site was for this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only know that the school of the blind was viewed as a sniping nest by the people and that there were ABiH soldiers close to the trench where the girls were. For the rest, I do not know where the confrontation line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see if I can try one more photograph. 1D528. And while we're waiting for this, in the information that was provided to you when you visited the location, did anyone mention the retirees' home or nursing home that was approximately 40 metres from the incident site?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing this building, but I don't recall any other information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you say you remember seeing this building, did you remember seeing this building nearby the incident site for this incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If nearby would be within 300 metres, I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's fair enough. Is the building and the damage to the building representative of what the surroundings of the incident site looked like or showed evidence of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean about as far as bushes are concerned, about gates, about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The damage. The damage to the building, the pockmarks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe this building looks worse than -- probably it's a different type of building than the apartment building that we just saw. This building, I believe, is built of solid bricks and the apartment building is usually of -- from the houses that I have seen in Bosnia, most of the houses have hollow bricks, and one bullet will have a bigger effect on it than on a brick -- a solid brick wall, as well as for the stucco on the walls, it doesn't necessarily represent the real damage. But this building does look worse than other buildings that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My information is that this is 40 metres, approximately, from the incident site, but it doesn't matter. I'll go with your within 300 metres. If the confrontation line and buildings with this type of damage are 300 metres from the incident site, can you, with a reasonable degree of professional scientific certainty, exclude the possibility that the victim in this case was wounded by cross-fire or fire emanating from the warring factions at the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't rely entirely on scientific certainty. I believe there are other factors. If I were a young girl, even if I was -- wanted to keep my shoes clean, which I believe I read in the -- in one of the witness statements, if there was shooting going on, I would not try to cross the street. So that it is not scientifically but it is pure logic, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, in your view, if you were a young girl and soldiers had told you not to go a particular way because it was dangerous, would you have gone?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I've read in the witness statement. But the line between people telling me where not to go and actual exchange of fire with bullets whizzing by, I believe that is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough, sir. I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have concluded with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break. Could you give us an indication, Ms. Hochhauser, as to how much time you would need after the break for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'll be able to give a more precise estimate at -- directly upon returning, but I would say approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that. Please consider what is necessary to be asked in re-examination. Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We whether take a break, and we will resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, you will now be re-examined by Ms. Hochhauser. Ms. Hochhauser, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, during your cross-examination, you were asked on several occasions about the -- whether the charts in the back of -- lists that you list in your report following the incidents included this -- the entire sum of everything that you considered for that incident. Did you also, in addition to what is in those charts -- excuse me, sorry. You also referenced in your responses certain videos and photographs. Did you also see videos taken with witness -- with victims and an OTP investigator, such as the one we saw in Court yesterday at 65 ter 22457?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And -- let's see. Okay. Also, earlier today, and this is in regard to incident F9, at temporary transcript page 41, lines 17 through 19, you were asked about, in particular, whether you would permit that uniformed soldiers would have been an appropriate and legitimate target for the opposing side to shoot at. In response, you stated: "If the uniformed soldiers would have been in the same view of the same picture for the shooter, then they -- well, I would agree that a uniformed soldier could present a legitimate target." And I would like to -- I would like, at this point, Your Honours, to show -- to add to the 65 ter exhibit list a statement of one of those witnesses, 65 ter 28627. And, Your Honours, for your information, this has been -- this is a document that is one of the subjects of the Prosecution's fifth 92 bis motion filed 6 September 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand you. You said you'd like to add the statement to the 65 ter list. Is that not included in the 92 bis motion? And even for a 92 bis witness, I would expect that the witness statement would already be on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not -- had not yet assigned it a 65 ter number, although it is a pending statement that's subject of one of those -- of that motion. Which is still pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're doing at this moment, so you are assigning a 65 ter number to that. It doesn't -- is yet, not yet, on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: It has been disclosed to the Defence. It is a subject of that pending 92 bis motion but it had not yet been assigned a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what are we supposed to do with it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness look at a portion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To look at a portion. Or would you like to ask questions about it? It is a bit unclear to me how you want to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I could simply proceed by quoting from it without showing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that would be -- if the Defence is then aware it has been -- it's disclosed material, and it arises now in cross-examination; therefore, please do as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Van der Weijden, referring back to that same portion of testimony about F9, and I'll refer to information that -- from a statement that you list in your chart in regard to F9, the statement of a witness dated 8 November 1995 in which -- and this is from one of the victims. In which she says: "Not from my place at about 1900 hours or 1930 hours, we arrived at a spot where we saw soldiers on the opposite of the street. They were at a balcony on the third floor and shouted at us." And this is the shouted warning that was referred to, that was discussed in the cross-examination, the shouted warning to the two girls about snipers in the area. So, Captain, my question for you, is: These soldiers on the third floor of the building on the opposite side of the street, and given the distance that's noted, the short distance that is noted in your report from the location in the school of the blind that you identified as the origin of fire, and the -- and the incident location where the girls were shot, if the shooter was aiming at soldiers in such a location, would you expect the soldiers to be in the same view of the shooter as the witness and her friend?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How -- reading these lines, I believe that the soldiers, if they would have been on the third floor of the building on the opposite side of the street, they've been on a balcony facing the square where the girls were also present. They wouldn't have been visible to the point of origin, which I think is the school of the blind. So they wouldn't even have been visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you now to yesterday's transcript, page 6544, at line 22, where you had the following question and answer: "Q. Would you agree with me that you cannot know if there are any other targets in the area on that day that may have been the intended target, which resulted in a missed shot that could have struck this victim in the manner we discussed before?" And you answered: "No, I do not agree." Can you explain or elaborate upon this answer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you point out in -- what incident is involved in this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I -- I don't believe that it was -- let me just turn to it. I don't believe that it was a specific incident. It was a general question. Do we see the -- let's see ...

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I -- I think I remember that we were discussing Spicaste Stijena at that time, Sharpstone. And, as I recall, there -- it was about the BiH lines down in the valley, if they could have been the intended target instead of the target, the further -- further in the valley. I think -- Could we check that? Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, if we could -- if we can go ... to the question before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's about the second of the Unscheduled Incidents, it seems, Spicaste Stijena. We find that on line 14: "If we can turn to the second of the Unscheduled Incidents." That was what the question was about. It was about a shot at a range of 850 to 950 metres. You said: "It is a difficult long-range shot." And then the question just quoted by Ms. Hochhauser was put to you. Ms. Hochhauser, any further questions on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Did -- did -- did being pointed to that enable you to clarify your answer or expand upon the answer when you said, No, I do not agree with Mr. Ivetic's proposition.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What -- because we -- I believe we were discussing the -- the ABiH lines compared to the VRS positions at that time. The difference between the ABiH lines and the incident site is that far apart that there is no -- there can be no stray shot or the -- the -- as people commonly refer to it, or a missed target. The -- it was the -- the only civilian target within that area. The military targets were further down, closer to Sharpstone, and shots fired at that direction or at those positions, then guns would have -- be elevated to an extreme level. It's close to zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just exclude any military target which is not on a fixed position close to the confrontation line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I concluded that that target was that far from the confrontation line, that there was no military target close to that -- not -- front line target close to the incident's location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that doesn't resolve the problem. Could there be two soldiers walking nearby, which is not a fixed position, at the confrontation line? Not to say that there's any evidence for that at this moment, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That might have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just do not know. You say -- as a matter of fact, you say it was the only civilian target you are aware of, where you have considered primarily fixed positions close to the confrontation lines. Is that how I have to understand your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. It is the only civilian target compared to the positions at the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to today's temporary transcript, page 13, lines 21 through 25, and in the context of the methods that might be used to overcome the visibility problems of an optical scope on a sniper rifle you were asked about whether you knew what equipment was available to either the snipers of the VRS or the Army of BiH. In connection with this line of questioning, can we please draw up on the monitor 65 ter 28490. And this is a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command order number 20/15-1244, signed by Stanislav Galic, dated 29 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, this is also one of the documents that was not identified as having been reviewed by the witness in his expert report and which was the subject of the objection to the, quote/unquote, 31 documents that was in the Defence response to the 94 bis submission for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it now apparently has become relevant on the basis of your cross-examination, which creates a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. I'm just bringing it to the record that this is one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm not seeing the document on the screen. Oh ... sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now let me just see ... yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I would draw your attention, Captain, to the paragraph labelled 1 on page 1 of this document, where it states that: "Each brigade set up a platoon-strength snipers group, 30 plus 1 soldiers. These should be supplied with sniper rifles, optical and IC infrared passive sights silencers." Is there any equipment mentioned in the extract that I've just read out that could be used to overcome visibility problems of an optical scope on a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe the infrared and passive sights would certainly be able to overcome low visibility concerning -- low-light visibility problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And as a follow-up to this document, I'd also like to draw up, please, 65 ter 28491. And if we could scroll down to the final paragraph on the first page, where it reads: "Thus far" -- It's the last sentence in the English. I'm sorry, I can't identify it in the B/C/S. "Thus far, the snipers from the subordinated units have been active mostly in pairs, in the areas of Trebevic, Hresa and Podgrab ..." And, again, I apologise for any mispronunciations. And, again, in the context of overcoming visibility problems of an optical scope on a sniper rifle, does the working in pairs have an impact on that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It most certainly would. As I have written in the report is that working in pairs enhances the effectivity of the -- of the sniper, since the spotter can support him with his optical sights. Or his -- his optics and, in general, binoculars or his spotting scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, just to say that you can't identify it in the B/C/S is not -- is it on this page? Let's have a look where it's supposed to be. I think it is at bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wasn't able to identify that particular sentence on the -- in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see the word "zrak," which immediately precedes the portion you read in the last paragraph on the first page. And Trebevic appears on the fifth line of the -- in that bullet point part on the first page. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And Captain, in fact, at yesterday's transcript, page -- it was -- I have here noted 650, but I -- that may have been the -- the temporary transcript which I noted down. But you were -- you were asked specifically a question about a portion of your report in which you identify that snipers work in pair -- are often found working in pairs. And the question read: "Among those items" -- Well, the full question read at page 4 in the English and page 6 of the B/C/S: "You outline tasks and deployments of the sniper and training of a sniper. And among those items you include several times the necessity of a sniper team to consist of two persons." So, again, I want to make sure that is in relation to your experience and knowledge as to NATO armies. And I see it's at transcript 6.520. And that you are not suggesting any expertise or knowledge of such factors in relation to the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of BiH. And so I would also like to ask you in regard to what is on -- what the document -- the document that is still on the monitor, 28491, where it says that the units have been mostly -- active mostly in pairs, what that suggests to you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would suggest that snipers are, in fact, using the same time of tactics as NATO armies, since working in pairs makes them more effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at this time, I'd like to tender, please, 28490 and 28491.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, it should be -- because I'm reading which suggests that snipers are, in fact, using the same type of tactics. Instead of attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that the witness has testified about it now, I don't see the -- if I can object. But, again, it's mixing and matching apples and oranges. Because the questions I asked were related to whether he had reviewed anything prior to issuing his report and had any knowledge thereof, and now we're pulling out one document that he hasn't seen until the courtroom, and it's being presented for something. So I have an objection to the manner in which it is being presented, but I do believe that the documents should be entered because the witness has testified about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, there seems to be no objection, so -- unless you want to -- to admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Well, no. Except that there is no objection to admission. But I would just say that actually the questions yesterday were to -- went directly to the weight of this witness's testimony based on his area of knowledge. And so the similarities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, yes. There's no objection. At the same time, I take it that you want to say that apples and pears are similar fruits of the same size; whereas, you are pointing at the difference between apples and pears. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 28490 becomes Exhibit P675; while 65 ter 28491 becomes Exhibit P676. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P675 and P676 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I think the witness made a correction of the transcription where the correction is not recorded correctly. I think. Page 36, line 6. If I understood you correctly, you said the same of -- type of tactics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And tactics is t-a-c-t-i-c-s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It was page 63. I misspoke. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now, finally, did you correct in this way, the language you used before, or did you correct the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I corrected the correction on the transcript of the language that I used before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 25229 on the monitor. Which is the programme for a sniper course in the VRS issued by the Republika Srpska Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, I believe you've had the opportunity to see this document before. But if we could -- if I could ask if we could just slowly turn to page 1 and then 2 so that the witness can recollect what it is he is looking at. And do you recall having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether the training course for snipers in the VRS run by the Republika Srpska is typical or atypical of the sniping curricula that you are familiar with from your experience?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subjects of the course would -- are certainly familiar -- of similar with other courses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, 65 ter 25229, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, on this one, there has been no basis for it to be admitted in whole. I mean, I don't even know how many pages this one is, Your Honour. But this witness, just by saying -- looking at one page and saying it appears to be consistent with what NATO courses teach doesn't meet, I think, the standards for admission of a document if it's being presented for the truth of the matters asserted therein.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would say that the witness has actually testified that he has seen the whole of the document. I just didn't take the time in court to flip through each page. And, again -- and I -- I don't want to the co-opt Your Honour's words, but I think we're having the same argument about the apples and the pears. I think the Defence has, in its cross-examination, made the point that he has knowledge -- or tried to make the point that this witness's knowledge is not based or not applicable to the Army of the Republika Srpska, and so I think that it's proper re-direct and proper comment from the witness to talk about -- to -- to put in evidence that it is similar and that it does jive with what he has testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two issues. The first one, whether what is written here has happened. That is a matter, part of the evaluation of the evidence giving weight to the evidence. The objection is denied. Mr. Ivetic, you have consistently challenged that training, education, many aspects of sniping in the former Yugoslavia, may have been -- in the Republika Srpska may have been different from what the witness told us was usual in other armies. This is a document which allows him to compare what was at least written. Now, Ms. Hochhauser, before we decide on the matter, the document is dated 1995. Do you have any further details? And, apart from that, it is an attachment number 7, I think, to another document. It was attached to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Annex number 7, it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would have to take a -- take a few moments to answer that question, so if -- if we could, if I could have the opportunity to provide you with that information at a later date and revisit the ... the issue, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P677, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P677 is marked for identification. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 28602 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, while it's coming up, you've had the opportunity to visit the Metalka building, have you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And that is the location that, in your opinion, was the origin of fire of several of the Scheduled Incidents? I believe 11, 12 -- at least 11, 12, and 14.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, can you recognise what's on the screen now? Do you recognise that view?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, I recognise the structures in the -- in the view, in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the likelihood -- we've heard on cross-examination about the possibility that victims of the incidents that you address in your report were hit by errant shots. And can you explain the likelihood of a range of deviation -- excuse me. Can you explain the range of deviation of a -- of a shooter from such a position as this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the shooter would use a 7.62 times 39 millimetre rifle or 7.62 times 51, 54, or the 7.9 at a range of a little over 300 metres, the point of aim, it -- it depends on the adjustments on the scope. But I believe that the deviation would be not more than 1 metre. But then he would have make -- made a -- big mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And this -- I'm sorry, you did say you recognised the location. Can you tell us what the location is? What you recognise --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the yellow building, which is the Holiday Inn, the hotel. And I recognise the street that runs between the Holiday Inn and the Metalka building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So I would like to tender this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 28602 shall be assigned Exhibit P678. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P678 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask one follow-up question in this context, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At -- for various incidents, you have pointed at witnesses saying it -- shots came from the Grbavica building, and you said that was impossible apart from how that building is identified, but because that seems not to be very specific. But then you always jump to the Metalka building. You say, There is a building in that area. And then you start explaining that -- you could have fired from there and hit the target. Have you also considered other buildings in the same area? Because you do not explain why you choose for the Metalka building rather than any other building which could serve as a substitute for the rejected Grbavica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Metalka building is at the end of the street. The street itself forms a natural tunnel, and so from the location where the -- the tram I believe just -- was hit just in front -- just before the Holiday Inn hotel, just before the S-curve in the tracks where the tram would have to slow down if travelling from west to east, there's only one building that has a direct view on that intersection that is -- in a tactical way and a technical way, the -- an option. So I took into account other buildings, but the only other buildings that would offer a technical possibility are the museum close to the street and the faculty. The buildings in the streets, they would -- it -- is where I have testified that shooters would have to lean out the windows and expose themselves to enemy positions in order to be able to fire at the location. So that is where -- how I ended up at the Metalka building. It's simply for me, it's the only option there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have excluded other options.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your report would have been complete if you would have said, Having considered all the possible buildings, I ended up that the Metalka building was the one who had a free view or a free line of sight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could ask you a follow-up clarification of the language that you used in your response to Judge Orie just now. You used the word "tunnel." "The street itself forms a natural tunnel." And I think you used that same word in describing the bridge incident when you were describing the water. Can you tell us what you mean by "a tunnel"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it comes more or less from a tunnel view. It's -- there are buildings on left and the right side and -- that forms -- yeah. It's a natural tunnel towards somewhere or from somewhere. So you are boxed in on the left and the right side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Captain, we've heard evidence in this proceeding for -- to the effect that there were trained snipers operating in the Grbavica area. How likely do you think it that a trained sniper would accidentally hit a tram in front of the Holiday Inn while firing from a position within the Metalka building?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not likely. For a trained sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And counsel was asking about the possibility of the victim of F1 being hit by an errant shot. Did you view the witness statements of the parents of the child, Mr. And Mrs. Pita, in relation to that incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a long time, but if the witness statements are listed in the evidence list that I provided, then I have read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, was there any indication of an ongoing fire-fight in that vicinity at the time the victim was struck?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that there was mentioning of a few shots earlier in the morning and that there was fog in the morning, but I don't -- I think I read ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. If I can ask you the question a different way. Would -- would information about whether other shots were heard or not heard be a factor that you would consider in whether -- in considering whether this -- whether the child was an intended target of the -- of the shooter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might be a factor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the shots were heard or there were impacts in the vicinity of the incident site, then those shots might have been intended for the target as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And what would you expect to hear if there was an ongoing return of fire between the two parties up on the ridge of -- of Baba Rock and in the cemetery of Baba Rock?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yeah. There was questioning about whether the bullet that struck Anisa Pita could have been the result of a volley of fire on -- between the -- the BiH and VRS positions up on Baba Rock. What would you expect to hear if there was -- if there was ongoing -- if return of fire between the two parties at the time that the victim was shot?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would hear different -- every -- the shots that would have been fired from the cemetery would sound different from the ones from Baba Stijena because of the -- the difference in distance. So you would be able to clearly distinguish between a fire-fight that wasn't in the -- in the direct area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And are there other factors that you would consider when examining whether somebody who was the victim was -- whether -- excuse me. When considering whether the victim that was struck was actually the intended target of a shooter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are -- there was the issue of identification that I will take into account. I believe for this instance that there is -- that the courtyard where the girl was is, it's not the easiest location to look at because it's -- it's -- it's a darker hole than the surroundings. So identification is something that I always take into account. But I also look if there are tactical positions or if they had been there nearby. So if they are mentioned in witness statements that there were soldiers close by, then that might be a factor that I would include in my research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to analyse your last answer and see what it really means. The question was whether the victim that was struck was actually the intended target of the shooter. Now, part of your answer was the issue of identification. Now, if the person struck would be a small child, would that be an intended shot at that target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think I misinterpreted the question the little bit. Identification is not something entirely relevant to the question. What I do consider is the actions of the target at the time of the incident -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still then, how could this tell you that the shooter was intending to target that person or that place? It depends, isn't it, if the shooter, let's just assume for argument's sake, that the shooter is not willing to act in accordance with the -- with the rules applicable, then if you shoot a small child, he may have intended to do so. If the shooter wanted to obey all the rules, then hitting a small child might be an indication that he was not intending to target that victim. So, therefore, how could you possibly say anything about the intentions of the shooter just by looking at what happens? If you say, It is a difficult shot, now, if you intended to shoot at that position, then it was intended and it took quite an effort to do that. If it was not intended, it was a shot fired just at random and happened to enter that place. So I do not either understand what Ms. Hochhauser is trying to elicit as evidence. Neither do I understand the logic of your answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I apologise if my question was confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: What I'm asking, lieutenant, is we -- sorry, Captain, is we spoke today and yesterday at greater length about this idea of errant shots or what the intended target was. And can you -- and also the deviation of a bullet as it -- as it leaves, and we also addressed the idea of ricochet. Can you tell us what the -- what the range of deviation is that we're talking about? For example, using any of the scheduled -- or any of the Scheduled Incidents as an example, what kind of range of deviation from the intended target would you expect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. Is that, again, a bad question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it is. Because what are -- are you talking about deviation caused by wind, by other such factors as listed by the witness, if the shooter was a skilled shooter; or are you talking about the quality of the shooter? An untrained person, would he usually stay within 2 metres from the target, would he not. These are two different questions, and, therefore, deviation is an unclear concept in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Judge. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, to some extent, the witness has given an answer in respect of a certain distance. He said, If you would miss by 1 metre, if a trained sniper would miss by 1 metre, he would have made quite a mistake. So that means that a trained sniper, apparently at the distance we were talking about, at that time, should well remain within 1 metre from his intended target. So, to some extent, the witness has answered that, but you always need outside influence or the skills of the shooter, and that is what you ignored in your question. Nevertheless, if the witness could comment on your question, or could comment on my observations, he is invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to comment that the distance we're talking about, that was on a different distance. So it was a shorter -- a shorter range. So 920 metres would, of course, have more -- there are more variables to be taken into account for such a shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for your patience. That concludes the -- the re-direct examination. There is -- I see Mr. Ivetic is on his feet. There is also the issue of still the offering of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Two or three questions that arise out of the re-direct, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, counsel asked you about the problems with optical sights, and by my recollection, and please correct me if I'm wrong, the optical sight problems that we discussed were with four times magnification, you could not see what a person is holding in their hands at distance greater than 800 metres, and the problem that the reticle on the optical sight can be an impediment to see things at 600 metres. Am I accurate in the topics that you and I discussed earlier this morning as to problems with optical sights?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely. I think I said it would be difficult to see what a person is holding and not excluding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My focus was on the 600 metres and the 800 metres. Is that the what we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser showed you some documents with some information as to some passive infrared sights. Am I correct, sir, that such sites are known as second generation sights and are good for up to 300 to 400 metres?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No more questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has no questions for you either, Mr. Van der Weijden, this concludes your evidence. I would like to thank you for coming to this court and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The tendering of the report itself is the remaining issue. Anything you'd like to add, Mr. Ivetic, to what was already in the written submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would strongly oppose the tender of the report into evidence as an expert report. Given what we have heard, the Defence would renew its objections as follows. An expert is expected to give his or her expert opinion in full transparency --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down for sake of interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. An expert is expected to give his or her expert opinion in full transparency of established or assumed facts that he or she relies upon and of the methods used when applying his or her knowledge, experience, or skills to form his or her expert opinion. This is the ruling of the Martic Trial Chamber on 13 January 2006, at paragraph 37, and the ruling of the Gotovina Trial Chamber from 27 August 2009 at paragraph 10. Given the responses by this witness that he can't remember what materials he had, that he either misplaced or gave back to the Prosecution the materials that were his source, that the underlying military handbooks can neither be identified with particularity, nor given to the Defence without clearance from the government, all these things go against full transparency of this report, a report, I might add, that is virtually devoid of footnotes, and we learn now is also based on unknown material the witness gathered from the Internet from unknown web sites that he was unable to identify for us. The jurisprudence is very clear that the sources for an expert report must be clearly indicated and accessible in order to allow the other party or the Trial Chamber to test or challenge the bases on which the expert witness has reached his or her conclusions. The jurisprudence says that in the absence of clear references to accessible sources, the Trial Chamber will treat the matter as the witness's personal opinion rather than an expert opinion. This is from the Milosevic Trial Court, a decision on the expert report of Robert Donja, 15 February 2007, at paragraph 8. And, in the same case, they had a Defence expert witness that had the same result, 21 August 2007, at paragraph 7; and is also from the Stanisic and Simatovic, the decision on the Prosecution's submission of the expert reports of Nina Tromp and Christian Neilsen pursuant to Rule 94 bis of 18 March 2008, at paragraph 9. There is -- here, there is little opportunity for the Defence experts to advise the Defence on the matters that are the bases for this witness's testimony when he cannot provide clear references to accessible sources. Accordingly, this report does not meet the test to be admitted as an expert report, and the testimony of this witness must be disqualified as expert in nature as a result thereof. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, anything you would like to briefly say about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly, Your Honour. The witness's report does, in fact, contain the source of the information that he relied upon. I think that when Mr. Ivetic refers to the testimony about certain sources that he had returned or that he couldn't completely identify, that -- that testimony is limited solely to the Unscheduled Incidents and not to the Scheduled Incidents, so I wanted to point that out to the Court. In addition, I would rely already on what's already been said in the written filings about his experience and his expertise in this area, but I would specifically like to address the argument, also, about the -- about these military handbooks and the use of the Internet for certain things. The witness testified that during the course of his -- of his schooling, there were military handbooks that, of course, formed the basis of some of his schooling as he received a military education that went on -- from which he went on to have a long career and -- in sniping and as a sniper instructor. The on-the-job training for which -- and experience for which is obviously a huge part of his qualifications, which has led to him being deemed an expert and accepted as an expert in four prior trials before this Tribunal. The military handbooks that he -- that Mr. Ivetic refers to, to me, I would submit, to the Chamber is the equivalent of asking a doctor who comes in to testify about DNA to submit his biology text that he -- that he was trained on in college for the basis of his original -- the basis of his original training from which he then went on and gained an expertise. So that's -- those are the only additional arguments that I would like to address in response to what Mr. Ivetic just raised orally in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will decide on the admission of the expert report of Mr. Van der Weijden in due course. We take the break. And is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Also prepared to address the Chamber on that initial matter with respect to that e-mail. I can do that now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About that e-mail. I think it would be better -- would you need much time for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: About two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About two minutes. Then, after the break, we'll ask that the witness be on stand by after the two minutes when we deal with the matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we turn into private session so that you can you make your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. When the next witness is escorted into the courtroom, I have one matter to raise -- no, two matters, as a matter of fact. Therefore, the witness might need a bit more patience. The first is the Defence has requested seven extra days to respond to the 92 ter motion for Witness RM120. That request is granted. Then there was an issue about scheduling for the 25th of January, a Friday, a videolink. Unfortunately, on that Friday the Judges are not available for extended sessions in the afternoon. First of all, it is always risky to schedule a video-conference witness on a Friday, because if something goes wrong, then he has to wait for the whole of the weekend. So, therefore, it is preferred to schedule witnesses not on Fridays if they are giving their testimony through videolink. There are a few possible solutions. The one is to postpone the evidence and to hear the testimony on another day. Another option would be that the parties would consider to what extent they can commit themselves to not going beyond the time available on that Friday, and if you'd be half an hour or one hour short, the Chamber would consider an extended session but not in the afternoon but by starting at an earlier point of time in the morning. To the extent the parties could resolve this matter, they're invited to do so and inform the Chamber [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... perhaps I will discuss it with the Defence and raise it with the Chamber again next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, we need to act urgently, because if the videolink cannot take place on the 25th, then the preparations should be changed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Before you give evidence in this court, Mr. Mandilovic, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. Could you please stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Mr. Mandilovic, we have limited time today. It's unfortunate, but we started later than expected. You'll now first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli. Ms. D'Ascoli is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, the interpreter is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interpreter is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Likely it is still on channel 4, which was for the previous witness. Can you now hear me in a language you understand? Still not. Is the volume okay? Is the channel okay? Channel ... Could you ... Can you now hear me in a language you understand? I see you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what your current profession is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Medical doctor, a specialist in the General Hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, do you remember providing a statement to the ICTY on the 24th of February, 2010, in Sarajevo, a statement that amalgamated evidence from your previous testimony before this Tribunal and previous statements you also gave with some additional observations, as well as comments made to certain medical documents? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28611, which is the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, once I see the document is on the screen before you, can I ask that you view the first page in the English version, and, in particular, the signature at the bottom of the page and indicate whether you recognise that signature.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, have you had an opportunity to read and review this statement and the exhibits that are referred to in the statement in preparation for your appearance today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, you also had some corrections and clarifications to your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28622 on our screens, please. This is a chart of corrections and clarifications that was prepared with the witness, Your Honours, and we circulated by e-mail to all the Defence and Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, now that the document is on the screen, do you recognise this document as the table of correction and clarification that was made with you in preparation for this -- for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can we go to page 2 also, please, of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is my signature, and I authorised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And does it accurately set out the corrections and clarifications that you wanted to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, with these corrections and clarifications, are you satisfied your statement is an accurate record of your evidence and what you experienced in so far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if you were asked today the same questions that you were asked when the statement was taken, would you give the same answers and provide the same information, in substance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm that you provided the information in your statement in accordance with the truth and that your statement is a truthful and accurate reflection of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders the 65 ter 28611, which is the witness statement, together with the 65 ter 28622, which is the table of correction and clarifications pursuant to Rule 92 ter as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whom in the Defence team I have to address? Mr. Stojanovic, no objections. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 28611 witness statement receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P679 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P679 is admitted. 65 ter 28622.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P680 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have also prepared a table of concordance for the 65 ter numbers and the incident numbers that are referred to in the witness statement because these are those of the Karadzic case, and this way the parties would have an easy way to refer to the correct one in our case, in the Mladic case. We have asked leave to this table to the 65 ter exhibit list, and I would now tender it as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will assist the Chamber and the parties. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I would give the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Which is 28608.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, did I understand it well that there's no objection to this table to be admitted? P681 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also note there are 39 exhibits associated to Mr. Mandilovic's statement. Upon review, the Prosecution will not tendered them all, but will seek to tender 25 of these documents. These are mostly hospital medical records that the witness has authenticated through his statement. These are -- he has reviewed them and authenticate them as discussed in paragraphs 117, 118, and 119 of the statement. Now, I will deal with this associated exhibits during the course of my examination, also taking into account the objections that the Defence has raised in their response to our 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And now with the Chamber's permission, I will summarise Dr. Mandilovic's evidence for the record and the public. Dr. Mandilovic is a surgeon and a former JNA medical officer. From 1982, he worked at the military Hospital in Sarajevo, which was renamed the state Hospital in May 1992 in conjunction with the JNA withdrawal from the hospital, which then became a civilian facility. Mr. Mandilovic left the JNA and remained working at the Sarajevo state hospital throughout the war, from 1992 to 1995. He describes the conditions of work at the hospital during the war, water and food shortages, medicine and oxygen shortages, power cuts, which all heavily impacted on the normal functioning of the hospital. He also describes how the hospital building was directly hit on several occasions, the southern side of the hospital receiving most of the damages. Dr. Mandilovic performed surgery on wounded patients on a daily basis from May 1992 until the end of the war. He was on duty at the state hospital on 28 August 1995 and treated casualties from scheduled shelling incident G18, also known as the Markale II incident. Dr. Mandilovic authenticates selected hospital records relating to scheduled sniping incidents F5, F9, F11 F13, and relating to scheduled shelling incidents G4, G6, G7, G8, G13, and G18. And that concludes the summary of the witness's evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. I'm looking at the clock. I don't think it makes much sense to start further questioning the witness for the last two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: It does not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, you have not answered yet many questions, but I nevertheless have to instruct you that you should not speak about your evidence, whether that is evidence given today or evidence still to be given next Monday, and we'd like to see you back Monday morning at 9.30 but in a different courtroom. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Monday, the 14th of January, at 9.30 in the morning, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
